items.question: Why not ArrayList?
items.answer: ArrayList stores object. Adding an int boxes it onto the heap. Reading requires a cast that can throw InvalidCastException. List<int> stores ints directly, the compiler rejects a string, and there is no box. C# generics are reified — typeof(List<int>) works at run time unlike TypeScript erasure.
followUps: What is reification versus Java type erasure?
What is generic sharing for reference type arguments?
items.sixtySeconds: ArrayList = object + boxing + casts. List<T> = compile-time T, reified constructed type, no box for structs.

items.question: Explain open versus closed generics and generic sharing.
items.answer: Open generic: List<> or typeof(List<>) — type parameter still unbound. Closed generic: List<string> — concrete type you instantiate. Static fields are per closed type, not shared across all T. Generic sharing: reference-type type arguments often share one JIT-compiled body; value types like int get separate specializations. Open generics appear in DI registration: typeof(IHandler<>).
followUps: Why is Counter<int>.Count independent of Counter<string>.Count?
items.sixtySeconds: Open = unbound T. Closed = List<string>. Statics per closed type. Reference T args share JIT code; value types specialize.

items.question: Name the important constraints and exclusion rules.
items.answer: class, class?, struct, notnull, unmanaged, new(), base type, interface, Enum, Delegate, and allows ref struct. At most one of struct/class/notnull/unmanaged first. new() last among ordinary constraints; cannot pair with struct or unmanaged. notnull warns, does not error. Required members block new(). allows ref struct is last and cannot combine with class.
followUps: Why can't a type with required members satisfy new()?
What does where T : U mean?
items.sixtySeconds: Constraints unlock members on T. struct and new() cannot combine. allows ref struct last. IEquatable for value equality on class-constrained T.

items.question: Why does == on class-constrained T fail for strings?
items.answer: == on a class-constrained type parameter uses reference identity unless constrained to IEquatable<T>. string overloads == for content, but T does not inherit that overload semantics. Same<string>(x, y) can be false for equal content. Fix: constrain to IEquatable<T> and call a.Equals(b).
followUps: Does this apply to record types?
items.sixtySeconds: class-constrained == is reference identity. Use IEquatable<T> for value equality. Classic string trap in generic Max/Same helpers.

items.question: IEnumerable<string> assigned to IEnumerable<object> — legal?
items.answer: Yes — IEnumerable<out T> is covariant because T only flows out. IList<string> to IList<object> is not — Add would break type safety. Action<object> as Action<string> is contravariance (in T). Value types do not participate: IEnumerable<int> is not IEnumerable<object>. Arrays are covariant but unsafe on write.
followUps: Why are arrays covariant but List<T> is not?
items.sixtySeconds: out = producer = covariant. in = consumer = contravariant. IList and List invariant. Value types excluded.

items.question: How would you model a Redis cache miss in a generic API?
items.answer: Not T? Get<T>(key) — null collapses miss, stored empty, and JsonException fault. Prefer bool TryGet<T>(key, out T value) with MaybeNullWhen(false), or CacheResult<T> with Hit/Miss/Fault factories. Log metrics by outcome, not null rate. Keep a small readonly struct; do not import a heavyweight Result library.
followUps: When is TryGet enough without Fault?
Why is unconstrained T? a poor miss signal?
items.sixtySeconds: Miss is not null. TryGet for hit/miss. CacheResult<T> for fault. Metrics by outcome on Redis paths.

items.question: How do C# generics differ from C++ templates and TypeScript generics?
items.answer: C++ templates expand per use at compile time. C# shares JIT code for reference type parameters and reifies closed types in metadata. TypeScript erases T before run time — no typeof(List<int>). C# List<int> and List<string> are distinct types; TypeScript List<T> is compile-time only. Do not say C# generates a new source file per T.
followUps: What does reification buy you in reflection?
Does Java behave like C# or TypeScript?
items.sixtySeconds: C# reified, shared JIT for ref T. TS erased. C++ template expansion. Not interchangeable answers.

items.question: When would you declare your own IProducer<out T> or IConsumer<in T>?
items.answer: When you design an API where T only flows out (read-only producer) or only in (callback consumer). The compiler rejects T in both input and output positions on a variant interface. Use invariance (no out/in) when T is both read and written — like a mutable buffer interface. IList<T> stays invariant for safety.
followUps: Can a class declare out T?
Give a production example of contravariance.
items.sixtySeconds: out for producers, in for consumers, invariant when T goes both ways. Only interfaces and delegates.

items.question: Static state on RedisCache<T> — one counter or many?
items.answer: Per closed type. RedisCache<int> and RedisCache<string> each get their own static fields. Assuming one shared static across all T is a common interview trap. Generic sharing applies to JIT code for reference type arguments, not to static field storage.
followUps: How does open generic DI registration relate?
items.sixtySeconds: Statics belong to the closed constructed type. Counter<int> and Counter<string> are independent.
